lead: The A320 and the B787 sit at opposite ends of civil power-system design. The A320 keeps a fixed-frequency 115 V AC (alternating current) supply at 400 Hz and a 28 V DC (direct current) supply from transformer rectifier units. The B787 uses a more-electric, bleedless layout: 235 V AC at variable frequency and 270 V DC. The reason for the higher voltage is cable weight and load growth. For the same power, a higher voltage needs less current, so thinner cables and lower copper loss. These two aircraft show how architecture choices follow from voltage, frequency and conversion.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for generation and protection, 3.2 for conversion, and 3.11 for bus arrangements.

sections.h3: A320: fixed frequency, two voltage levels

blocks.text: A320: fixed frequency, two voltage levels. The A320 has two engine-driven integrated drive generators. An integrated drive generator (IDG) is a generator with a built-in constant-speed drive, so the generator turns at a speed that gives 115 V AC at 400 Hz even when the engine speed changes. Each IDG is rated 90 kVA. The rating is in kVA, apparent power, not kW. A generator control unit (GCU) regulates the generator field, monitors faults and controls the generator contactor that connects the IDG to its AC bus. A contactor is a heavy-duty relay. A bus tie contactor can join the two main AC buses when one generator is off.

An auxiliary power unit (APU) generator of similar size supplies AC power on the ground and in flight as a backup. In an all-generator failure, a ram air turbine (RAT) drives a small emergency generator for essential loads; see 3.4. Transformer rectifier units (TRUs) convert 115 V AC to 28 V DC for DC buses and battery charging. Nickel-cadmium batteries supply DC power before engine start and bridge short interruptions. The result is a conventional split bus system, with AC and DC essential buses kept alive by contactor logic.

sections.h3: B787: variable frequency and more electric

blocks.text: B787: variable frequency and more electric. The B787 removes engine bleed air for cabin pressurisation and uses electrical power for more loads. Each engine carries two large starter-generators, each rated 250 kVA. A starter-generator is a machine that starts the engine and then generates electricity. It produces 235 V AC at variable frequency, about 360 Hz to 800 Hz, as engine speed changes. No constant-speed drive is fitted, so the AC bus frequency is not fixed.

Two APU starter-generators supply ground power and backup. Transformer rectifier units convert 235 V AC to 270 V DC. Lithium-ion batteries provide emergency and ground power. The RAT supplies essential buses when all normal sources fail. Every load on the variable-frequency bus must accept the full 360-800 Hz range; this is the key design rule. Motors, transformers and power supplies are specified for that range. The figure shows this chain.

blocks.where: P is real power in watts; V_L is line voltage in volts; I_L is line current in amperes; cos φ is power factor.

blocks.text: At unity power factor, I_L = P/(√3 V_L). Cable copper loss per phase is I_L² R, so total three-phase loss is 3 I_L² R. For the same P, raising V_L lowers I_L and lowers loss as 1/V_L². That is why 235 V and 270 V DC save copper weight and reduce loss, but they demand new insulation, connectors and load design.

examples.question: A 100 kW balanced three-phase load at unity power factor is supplied first at 115 V line voltage and then at 235 V line voltage. The same three-core cable is used in both cases. Find the line current in each case and the ratio of cable copper loss. Use √3 = 1.732.
steps: For a balanced three-phase load, I_L = P/(√3 V_L cos φ). At 115 V: I_L1 = 100000/(1.732 × 115) = 502.1 A.
Total three-phase copper loss is 3 I_L² R, with R the resistance per phase. The same cable gives the same R. Loss ratio = (I_L1/I_L2)² = (502.1/245.8)² = 4.17, about 4.2.
examples.answer: The line currents are 502.1 A at 115 V and 245.8 A at 235 V; the higher voltage cuts copper loss by a factor of about 4.2.

traps: Do not say the B787 needs a constant-speed drive. Its AC bus is variable frequency by design; every load must accept 360-800 Hz.
Do not mix 235 V AC with 270 V DC. The first is generation and AC distribution; the second is a DC bus made by TRUs.
The A320's 115 V is fixed at 400 Hz because the IDG holds generator speed constant; the engine speed itself is not constant.
Generator ratings in kVA are apparent power, not kW. At a power factor below one, the kW available is lower than the kVA rating.
The RAT is an emergency source, not a normal source for engine start or ground power.

quiz.q: State the A320 main AC generator rating, voltage and frequency.
quiz.a: 90 kVA, 115 V AC, 400 Hz, one per engine, driven through an IDG.

quiz.q: What DC bus voltage does the B787 make from its TRUs?
Why does the B787 not need a constant-speed drive?
quiz.a: The generator output is allowed to vary in frequency with engine speed (360-800 Hz); loads are designed to accept that range, so no fixed-speed gearbox is needed.

quiz.q: A balanced three-phase 50 kW load at unity power factor is fed at 235 V line voltage. Find line current. Use √3 = 1.732.
For the same cable and same real power, compare copper loss at 115 V and 235 V.
quiz.a: Loss is proportional to 1/V², so the ratio is (235/115)² = 4.18; the 235 V case has about one-quarter the loss.

quiz.q: Why is a variable-frequency bus a system-wide design rule, not just a generator change?
quiz.a: Every load, transformer, motor and power supply connected to that bus must tolerate 360-800 Hz; otherwise it may overheat, lose regulation or fail.

quiz.q: What does a TRU do in both architectures?
quiz.a: It converts AC bus power to DC bus power: 115 V AC to 28 V DC in the A320, 235 V AC to 270 V DC in the B787.

beyond: Not for the exam. More-electric aircraft research pushes voltage higher to cut cable weight and to power bleedless cabins, electric brakes and electric engine accessories. Wide-bandgap devices such as silicon carbide and gallium nitride make high-voltage DC conversion lighter. Newer architectures study 540 V DC and 230 V AC variable-frequency buses. Search for more electric aircraft, variable frequency AC power and 270 V DC avionics.
